cards.title: Paso 1: Enunciado y Notación s_n(x) y t_n(x)
cards.front_html:
Teorema: $\lim_{n \to \infty} \left(1 + \frac{x}{n}\right)^n = \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!}$ para $x \ge 0$.
Paso 1: Definición de secuencias parciales.
cards.back_html:
Para $x \ge 0$, definimos la suma parcial de la serie $s_n(x)$ y el término binomial $t_n(x)$:
$$s_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n \frac{x^k}{k!}, \quad t_n(x) = \left(1 + \frac{x}{n}\right)^n$$

cards.title: Paso 2: Expansión Binomial y Cota Superior
cards.front_html: Paso 2: Expansión binomial de $t_n(x)$ y cota superior por $s_n(x)$ ($x \ge 0$)
cards.back_html:
Expandiendo $t_n(x)$ por el teorema del binomio:
$$t_n(x) = \sum_{k=0}^n\binom{n}{k}\frac{x^k}{n^k}=\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{1}{k!}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right) \cdot x^k$$
Como $x \ge 0$ y cada factor $\left(1 - \frac{i}{n}\right) \lt 1$, acotamos cada término por arriba:
$$t_n(x) \le s_n(x)$$

cards.title: Paso 3: Desigualdad con Limsup
cards.front_html: Paso 3: Límite superior.
cards.back_html:
Tomando $\limsup_{n\to\infty}$ en la desigualdad $t_n(x) \le s_n(x)$:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} t_n(x) \le \lim_{n\to\infty} s_n(x)$$

cards.title: Paso 4: Truncamiento Truncado a m Términos
cards.front_html: Paso 4: Truncamiento a $m$ términos. ($m \le n$)
cards.back_html:
Para cualquier entero fijo $m \le n$, truncamos la suma de $t_n(x)$ a los primeros $m$ términos. Como todos los términos omitidos son $\ge 0$ (pues $x \ge 0$):
$$t_n(x) \ge \sum_{k=0}^m \frac{1}{k!}\prod_{i=0}^{k-1}\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right) \cdot x^k$$

cards.title: Paso 5: Límites n -> infty y m -> infty
cards.front_html: Paso 5: Límites en $n \to \infty, m \to \infty$ y conclusión.
cards.back_html:
Manteniendo $m$ fijo y tomando $n \to \infty$, como es una suma finita de $m$ términos, los factores $(1 - j/n) \to 1$:
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} t_n(x) \ge s_m(x)$$
Tomando ahora el límite $m \to \infty$:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} s_n(x) \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} t_n(x)$$
Como $$\lim_{n\to\infty} s_n(x) \le \liminf t_n(x) \le \limsup t_n(x) \le \lim_{n\to\infty} s_n(x)$$ Se concluye para $x \ge 0$: $$\lim_{n\to\infty} t_n(x) = \lim_{n\to\infty} s_n(x)$$

cards.title: Remark General & Part (a): Límite de 1/n^p
cards.front_html:
General Remark: If $0 \le x_n \le s_n$ for $n \ge N$, where $N$ is fixed, and if $s_n \to 0$, then $x_n \to 0$.

Theorem 3.20(a): If $p \gt 0$, prove that:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n^p} = 0$$
cards.back_html:
Take $n \gt (1/\varepsilon)^{1/p}$. (Note that the Archimedean property of the real number system is used here.)

Then for all $n \ge N \gt (1/\varepsilon)^{1/p}$:
$$n^p \gt \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \implies 0 \lt \frac{1}{n^p} \lt \varepsilon$$
Hence $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n^p} = 0$.

cards.title: Part (b): Límite de p^(1/n)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.20(b): If $p \gt 0$, prove that:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{p} = 1$$
cards.back_html:
• If $p \gt 1$: Put $x_n = \sqrt[n]{p} - 1$. Then $x_n \gt 0$, and by the Binomial Theorem:
    $$1 + n x_n \le (1 + x_n)^n = p$$
    so that:
    $$0 \lt x_n \le \frac{p - 1}{n}$$
    Hence $x_n \to 0$ (since $\frac{p-1}{n} \to 0$ by part (a)), so $\sqrt[n]{p} \to 1$.
  • If $p = 1$: (b) is trivial.
  • If $0 \lt p \lt 1$: The result is obtained by taking reciprocals of $\sqrt[n]{1/p} \to 1$.

cards.title: Part (c): Límite de n^(1/n)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.20(c): Prove that:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{n} = 1$$
cards.back_html:
Put $x_n = \sqrt[n]{n} - 1$. Then $x_n \ge 0$, and by the Binomial Theorem:
$$n = (1 + x_n)^n \ge \frac{n(n-1)}{2} x_n^2$$
Hence:
$$0 \le x_n \le \sqrt{\frac{2}{n - 1}} \quad (n \ge 2)$$
Since $\sqrt{\frac{2}{n-1}} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, we get $x_n \to 0$, so $\lim_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{n} = 1$.

cards.title: Part (d): Límite de n^alpha / (1+p)^n
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.20(d): If $p \gt 0$ and $\alpha$ is real, prove that:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n^\alpha}{(1+p)^n} = 0$$
cards.back_html:
Let $k$ be an integer such that $k \gt \alpha, k \gt 0$. For $n \gt 2k$:
$$(1 + p)^n \gt \binom{n}{k} p^k = \frac{n(n-1)\dots(n-k+1)}{k!} p^k \gt \frac{n^k p^k}{2^k k!}$$
Hence:
$$0 \lt \frac{n^\alpha}{(1+p)^n} \lt \frac{2^k k!}{p^k} n^{\alpha - k} \quad (n \gt 2k)$$
Since $\alpha - k \lt 0$, $n^{\alpha - k} \to 0$ by part (a). Hence $\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{n^\alpha}{(1+p)^n} = 0$.

cards.title: Part (e): Límite de x^n para |x| < 1
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.20(e): If $|x| \lt 1$, prove that:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} x^n = 0$$
cards.back_html:
Take $\alpha = 0$ in part (d).

Specifically:
  • If $x = 0$, $x^n = 0 \to 0$.
  • If $0 \lt |x| \lt 1$, write $\frac{1}{|x|} = 1 + p$ with $p \gt 0$. Then $|x|^n = \frac{1}{(1+p)^n}$.

By part (d) with $\alpha = 0$, $\frac{1}{(1+p)^n} \to 0 \implies |x|^n \to 0 \implies \lim_{n\to\infty} x^n = 0$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.22: Cauchy Criterion for Series
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.22 (Cauchy Criterion for Series):
Prove that $\sum a_n$ converges if and only if for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ there is an integer $N$ such that:
$$\left| \sum_{k=n}^m a_k \right| \le \varepsilon \quad \text{if } m \ge n \ge N$$
cards.back_html:
Let $s_m = \sum_{k=1}^m a_k$ be the sequence of partial sums.

The series $\sum a_n$ converges $\iff$ the sequence $(s_m)$ converges.

By the Cauchy criterion for sequences (Theorem 3.11), $(s_m)$ converges $\iff$ for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$ there is an integer $N$ such that $|s_m - s_{n-1}| \le \varepsilon$ whenever $m \ge n \ge N$.

Since $s_m - s_{n-1} = \sum_{k=n}^m a_k$, the condition $|s_m - s_{n-1}| \le \varepsilon$ becomes:
$$\left| \sum_{k=n}^m a_k \right| \le \varepsilon$$

cards.title: Theorem 3.23: Term Limit Zero & Harmonic Counterexample
cards.front_html: Theorem 3.23: If $\sum a_n$ converges, prove that $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$. Is $a_n \to 0$ sufficient for convergence?
cards.back_html:
By taking $m = n$ in the Cauchy criterion (6) of Theorem 3.22:
$$|a_n| \le \varepsilon \quad (n \ge N)$$
In other words, $\lim_{n\to\infty} a_n = 0$.

Counterexample: The condition $a_n \to 0$ is NOT sufficient to ensure convergence of $\sum a_n$. For instance, the harmonic series $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}$ diverges (refer to Theorem 3.28).

cards.title: Theorem 3.24: Bounded Partial Sums for Non-negative Series
cards.front_html: Theorem 3.24: Prove that a series of non-negative terms converges if and only if its partial sums form a bounded sequence.
cards.back_html:
Let $s_n = \sum_{k=1}^n a_k$. Since $a_n \ge 0$, $s_n = s_{n-1} + a_n \ge s_{n-1}$, so the sequence of partial sums $(s_n)$ is monotonic increasing.

By Theorem 3.14 (monotonic sequences), a monotonic sequence of real numbers converges if and only if it is bounded.

Hence, $\sum a_n$ converges $\iff$ its partial sums form a bounded sequence.

cards.title: Theorem 3.25: The Comparison Test
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.25 (Comparison Test):
(a) If $|a_n| \le c_n$ for $n \ge N_0$, where $N_0$ is some fixed integer, and if $\sum c_n$ converges, then $\sum a_n$ converges.
(b) If $a_n \ge d_n \ge 0$ for $n \ge N_0$, and if $\sum d_n$ diverges, then $\sum a_n$ diverges.

Prove both (a) and (b):
cards.back_html:
Proof of (a): Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, there exists $N \ge N_0$ such that $m \ge n \ge N$ implies $\sum_{k=n}^m c_k \le \varepsilon$, by the Cauchy criterion. Hence:
$$\left| \sum_{k=n}^m a_k \right| \le \sum_{k=n}^m |a_k| \le \sum_{k=n}^m c_k \le \varepsilon$$
and (a) follows by Theorem 3.22.

Proof of (b): (b) follows from (a) by contrapositive, for if $\sum a_n$ converges, so must $\sum d_n$ (note that (b) also follows from Theorem 3.24).

cards.title: Theorem 3.26: Geometric Series
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.26 (Geometric Series):
Prove that if $0 \le x \lt 1$, then:
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty x^n = \frac{1}{1-x}$$
and if $x \ge 1$, the series diverges.
cards.back_html:
If $x \ne 1$, the partial sums are:
$$s_n = \sum_{k=0}^n x^k = \frac{1 - x^{n+1}}{1-x}$$
For $0 \le x \lt 1$, $x^{n+1} \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$, so $\lim s_n = \frac{1}{1-x}$.

For $x = 1$, we get $1 + 1 + 1 + \dots$, which evidently diverges.
For $x \gt 1$, $x^{n+1} \to \infty$, so $s_n \to \infty$ and the series diverges.

cards.title: Theorem 3.27: Cauchy Condensation Test — Setup & Upper Bound
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.27 (Cauchy Condensation Test) — Setup & Upper Bound:
Suppose $a_1 \ge a_2 \ge a_3 \ge \dots \ge 0$. Prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$ converges if and only if $\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^k a_{2^k}$ converges.

Paso 1: Definir las sumas parciales y demostrar $s_n \le t_k$ para $n \lt 2^k$:
cards.back_html:
By Theorem 3.24, it suffices to consider boundedness of partial sums.
Let:
$$s_n = a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n$$$$t_k = a_1 + 2a_2 + \dots + 2^k a_{2^k}$$
For $n \lt 2^k$, grouping terms:
$$s_n \le a_1 + (a_2 + a_3) + \dots + (a_{2^k} + \dots + a_{2^{k+1}-1}) \le a_1 + 2a_2 + \dots + 2^k a_{2^k} = t_k$$
so that:
$$s_n \le t_k$$

cards.title: Theorem 3.27: Cauchy Condensation Test — Lower Bound & Conclusion
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.27 (Cauchy Condensation Test) — Lower Bound & Conclusion:
Paso 2: Demostrar $2 s_n \ge t_k$ para $n \gt 2^k$ y concluir el teorema:
cards.back_html:
On the other hand, for $n \gt 2^k$, grouping terms:
$$s_n \ge a_1 + a_2 + (a_3 + a_4) + \dots + (a_{2^{k-1}+1} + \dots + a_{2^k}) \ge \frac{1}{2} a_1 + a_2 + 2a_4 + \dots + 2^{k-1} a_{2^k} = \frac{1}{2} t_k$$
so that:
$$2 s_n \ge t_k$$
By $s_n \le t_k$ and $t_k \le 2 s_n$, the sequences $\{s_n\}$ and $\{t_k\}$ are either both bounded or both unbounded. This completes the proof.

cards.title: Theorem 3.28: p-series Test
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.28 (p-series Test):
Prove that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^p}$ converges if $p \gt 1$ and diverges if $p \le 1$.
cards.back_html:
• If $p \le 0$, $a_n = 1/n^p \nrightarrow 0$, so divergence follows from Theorem 3.23.
  • If $p \gt 0$, Theorem 3.27 is applicable to the decreasing sequence $a_n = 1/n^p$, leading to the condensed series:
    $$\sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^k \cdot \frac{1}{2^{kp}} = \sum_{k=0}^\infty 2^{(1-p)k}$$
    Now $2^{1-p} \lt 1 \iff 1 - p \lt 0 \iff p \gt 1$. The result follows by comparison with the geometric series (take $x = 2^{1-p}$ in Theorem 3.26).

cards.title: Theorem 3.29: Logarithmic p-series Test
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.29 (Logarithmic p-series Test):
Prove that if $p \gt 1$, $\sum_{n=2}^\infty \frac{1}{n (\log n)^p}$ converges; if $p \le 1$, the series diverges.
cards.back_html:
The monotonicity of the logarithmic function implies that $\{\log n\}$ increases. Hence $\{1 / (n \log n)^p\}$ decreases, and we can apply Theorem 3.27 to the series:
$$\sum_{k=1}^\infty 2^k \cdot \frac{1}{2^k (\log 2^k)^p} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{(k \log 2)^p} = \frac{1}{(\log 2)^p} \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k^p}$$
Theorem 3.29 follows directly from Theorem 3.28.

cards.title: Theorem 3.33: Root Test — Statement & Proof of (a)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.33 (Root Test) — Statement & Proof of (a):
Given $\sum a_n$, put $\alpha = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}$.
Enunciar las 3 partes y demostrar la parte (a) ($\alpha \lt 1 \implies$ convergencia):
cards.back_html:
Enunciado:
  • (a) If $\alpha \lt 1$, $\sum a_n$ converges;
  • (b) If $\alpha \gt 1$, $\sum a_n$ diverges;
  • (c) If $\alpha = 1$, the test gives no information.

Demostración de (a):
If $\alpha \lt 1$, choose $\beta$ so that $\alpha \lt \beta \lt 1$, and an integer $N$ such that $\sqrt[n]{|a_n|} \lt \beta$ for $n \ge N$ (by Theorem 3.17(b)).

That is, $n \ge N$ implies $|a_n| \lt \beta^n$. Since $0 \lt \beta \lt 1$, $\sum \beta^n$ converges (geometric series). Convergence of $\sum a_n$ follows now from the comparison test.

cards.title: Theorem 3.33: Root Test — Proof of (b) & (c)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.33 (Root Test) — Proof of (b) & (c):
Demostrar (b) ($\alpha \gt 1 \implies$ divergencia) y (c) ($\alpha = 1 \implies$ inconcluso):
cards.back_html:
Demostración de (b):
If $\alpha \gt 1$, by Theorem 3.17, there is a subsequence $\{n_k\}$ such that $\sqrt[n_k]{|a_{n_k}|} \to \alpha$.

Hence $|a_n| \gt 1$ for infinitely many values of $n$, so that the condition $a_n \to 0$, necessary for convergence of $\sum a_n$, does not hold (Theorem 3.23).

Demostración de (c):
Consider the series $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ and $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$. For each of these series $\alpha = 1$, but the first diverges, while the second converges.

cards.title: Theorem 3.34: Ratio Test — Statement & Proof of (a)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.34 (Ratio Test) — Statement & Proof of (a):
Enunciar el criterio de la razón y demostrar la parte (a) ($\limsup \left|\frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n}\right| \lt 1 \implies$ convergencia):
cards.back_html:
Enunciado: The series $\sum a_n$:
  • (a) converges if $\limsup_{n\to\infty} \left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| \lt 1$,
  • (b) diverges if $\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| \ge 1$ for $n \ge n_0$, where $n_0$ is fixed.

Demostración de (a):
If condition (a) holds, we can find $\beta \lt 1$, and an integer $N$, such that $\left| \frac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right| \lt \beta$ for $n \ge N$. In particular:
$$|a_{N+1}| \lt \beta |a_N|, \quad |a_{N+2}| \lt \beta |a_{N+1}| \lt \beta^2 |a_N|, \dots, |a_{N+p}| \lt \beta^p |a_N|$$
That is, $|a_n| \lt |a_N| \beta^{-N} \cdot \beta^n$ for $n \ge N$, and (a) follows from the comparison test, since $\sum \beta^n$ converges.

cards.title: Theorem 3.34: Ratio Test — Proof of (b) & Note on Limit 1
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.34 (Ratio Test) — Proof of (b) & Note:
Demostrar (b) y explicar por qué la razón igual a 1 no da información:
cards.back_html:
Demostración de (b):
If $|a_{n+1}| \ge |a_n|$ for $n \ge n_0$, it is easily seen that the condition $a_n \to 0$ does not hold, and (b) follows.

Note: The knowledge that $\lim |a_{n+1}/a_n| = 1$ implies nothing about the convergence of $\sum a_n$. The series $\sum \frac{1}{n}$ and $\sum \frac{1}{n^2}$ demonstrate this.

cards.title: Theorem 3.37: Relation between Ratio and Root Test — Setup
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.37 (Ratio vs Root Test) — Setup:
For any sequence $\{c_n\}$ of positive numbers:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{c_n} \le \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}$$
Paso 1: Planteamiento de la demostración e iteración de desigualdades:
cards.back_html:
Put $\alpha = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}$.

If $\alpha = +\infty$, there is nothing to prove. If $\alpha$ is finite, choose $\beta \gt \alpha$. There is an integer $N$ such that $\frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n} \le \beta$ for $n \ge N$.

In particular, for any $p \gt 0$:
$$c_{N+k+1} \le \beta c_{N+k} \quad (k = 0, 1, \dots, p-1)$$
Multiplying these inequalities, we obtain:
$$c_{N+p} \le \beta^p c_N \implies c_n \le c_N \beta^{-N} \cdot \beta^n \quad (n \ge N)$$

cards.title: Theorem 3.37: Relation between Ratio and Root Test — Conclusion
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.37 (Ratio vs Root Test) — Conclusion:
Paso 2: Tomar raíz $n$-ésima y aplicar el Teorema 3.20(b) para concluir el teorema:
cards.back_html:
Taking $n$-th roots of $c_n \le c_N \beta^{-N} \cdot \beta^n$:
$$\sqrt[n]{c_n} \le \sqrt[n]{c_N \beta^{-N}} \cdot \beta$$
So that:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{c_n} \le \beta$$
by Theorem 3.20(b) (since $\sqrt[n]{c_N \beta^{-N}} \to 1$).

Since $\limsup \sqrt[n]{c_n} \le \beta$ is true for every $\beta \gt \alpha$, we have:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{c_n} \le \alpha = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \frac{c_{n+1}}{c_n}$$

cards.title: Theorem 3.39: Power Series & Radius of Convergence
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.39 (Power Series Convergence Theorem):
Given the power series $\sum c_n z^n$, put:
$$\alpha = \limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{|c_n|}, \quad R = \frac{1}{\alpha}$$
(If $\alpha = 0$, $R = +\infty$; if $\alpha = +\infty$, $R = 0$.)
Prove that $\sum c_n z^n$ converges if $|z| \lt R$, and diverges if $|z| \gt R$.
cards.back_html:
Put $a_n = c_n z^n$, and apply the root test (Theorem 3.33):
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|} = |z| \limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{|c_n|} = \frac{|z|}{R}$$
By the root test:
  • If $\frac{|z|}{R} \lt 1 \iff |z| \lt R$, the series converges.
  • If $\frac{|z|}{R} \gt 1 \iff |z| \gt R$, the series diverges.

Note: $R$ is called the radius of convergence of $\sum c_n z^n$.

cards.title: Examples 3.40: Radius of Convergence Examples
cards.front_html:
Examples 3.40: State the radius of convergence $R$ and boundary behavior for the following power series:
(a) $\sum n^n z^n$
(b) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n!}$
(c) $\sum z^n$
(d) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n}$
(e) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n^2}$
cards.back_html:
• (a) $\sum n^n z^n$: $\alpha = \limsup n = +\infty \implies R = 0$.
  • (b) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n!}$: $R = +\infty$ (by ratio test: $\frac{|z|}{n+1} \to 0 \lt 1$).
  • (c) $\sum z^n$: $R = 1$. Diverges for $|z|=1$ since $z^n \nrightarrow 0$.
  • (d) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n}$: $R = 1$. Diverges at $z = 1$ (harmonic series); converges for all other $z$ on $|z| = 1$ (Theorem 3.44).
  • (e) $\sum \frac{z^n}{n^2}$: $R = 1$. Converges for all $z$ on $|z| = 1$ by comparison ($|z^n/n^2| = 1/n^2$).

cards.title: Theorem 3.41: Partial Summation Formula (Summation by Parts)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.41 (Partial Summation Formula / Summation by Parts):
Given two sequences $\{a_n\}, \{b_n\}$, put $A_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k$ for $n \ge 0$, and $A_{-1} = 0$.
Prove that if $0 \le p \le q$, then:
$$\sum_{n=p}^q a_n b_n = \sum_{n=p}^{q-1} A_n (b_n - b_{n+1}) + A_q b_q - A_{p-1} b_p$$
cards.back_html:
Noting $a_n = A_n - A_{n-1}$:
$$\sum_{n=p}^q a_n b_n = \sum_{n=p}^q (A_n - A_{n-1}) b_n = \sum_{n=p}^q A_n b_n - \sum_{n=p-1}^{q-1} A_n b_{n+1}$$
Rearranging terms:
$$\sum_{n=p}^q a_n b_n = \sum_{n=p}^{q-1} A_n (b_n - b_{n+1}) + A_q b_q - A_{p-1} b_p$$
This is the partial summation formula, particularly useful when $\{b_n\}$ is monotonic.

cards.title: Theorem 3.42: Dirichlet's Test for Convergence
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.42 (Dirichlet's Test):
Suppose:
(a) the partial sums $A_n$ of $\sum a_n$ form a bounded sequence ($|A_n| \le M$);
(b) $b_0 \ge b_1 \ge b_2 \ge \dots$;
(c) $\lim_{n\to\infty} b_n = 0$.
Prove that $\sum a_n b_n$ converges.
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, choose $N$ such that $b_N \le \frac{\varepsilon}{2M}$. For $N \le p \le q$, using summation by parts:
$$\left| \sum_{n=p}^q a_n b_n \right| = \left| \sum_{n=p}^{q-1} A_n (b_n - b_{n+1}) + A_q b_q - A_{p-1} b_p \right| \le M \left[ \sum_{n=p}^{q-1} (b_n - b_{n+1}) + b_q + b_p \right] = 2 M b_p \le 2 M b_N \le \varepsilon$$
(noting $b_n - b_{n+1} \ge 0$). Convergence follows from the Cauchy criterion (Theorem 3.22).

cards.title: Theorem 3.43: Leibniz Alternating Series Test
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.43 (Leibniz Alternating Series Test):
Suppose:
(a) $|c_1| \ge |c_2| \ge |c_3| \ge \dots$;
(b) $c_{2m-1} \ge 0, c_{2m} \le 0$ ($m=1,2,3,\dots$);
(c) $\lim_{n\to\infty} c_n = 0$.
Prove that $\sum c_n$ converges.
cards.back_html:
Apply Theorem 3.42 with $a_n = (-1)^{n+1}$ and $b_n = |c_n|$.

The partial sums $A_n$ of $(-1)^{n+1}$ are bounded by 1 ($|A_n| \le 1$). Hypotheses (b) and (c) of Theorem 3.42 are satisfied by $b_n = |c_n| \downarrow 0$.

Thus $\sum c_n = \sum a_n b_n$ converges.

cards.title: Theorem 3.44: Convergence on the Boundary Circle |z| = 1
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.44 (Boundary Convergence of Power Series):
Suppose the radius of convergence of $\sum c_n z^n$ is 1, and suppose $c_0 \ge c_1 \ge c_2 \ge \dots$, $\lim_{n\to\infty} c_n = 0$.
Prove that $\sum c_n z^n$ converges at every point on $|z|=1$, except possibly at $z = 1$.
cards.back_html:
Put $a_n = z^n, b_n = c_n$. For $|z|=1$ and $z \ne 1$:
$$|A_n| = \left| \sum_{m=0}^n z^m \right| = \left| \frac{1 - z^{n+1}}{1 - z} \right| \le \frac{2}{|1 - z|}$$
So the partial sums $A_n$ form a bounded sequence for each fixed $z \ne 1$ on the unit circle.

The hypotheses of Theorem 3.42 are satisfied, hence $\sum c_n z^n$ converges.

cards.title: Definition & Theorem 3.45: Absolute Convergence
cards.front_html:
Definition & Theorem 3.45 (Absolute Convergence):
Definition: The series $\sum a_n$ is said to converge absolutely if $\sum |a_n|$ converges.

Theorem 3.45: Prove that if $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely, then $\sum a_n$ converges.
cards.back_html:
The assertion follows from the triangle inequality:
$$\left| \sum_{k=n}^m a_k \right| \le \sum_{k=n}^m |a_k|$$
Since $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely, $\sum |a_n|$ satisfies the Cauchy criterion (Theorem 3.22): for any $\varepsilon \gt 0$, $\sum_{k=n}^m |a_k| \le \varepsilon$ for $m \ge n \ge N$.

By the inequality above, $\left| \sum_{k=n}^m a_k \right| \le \varepsilon$, so $\sum a_n$ satisfies the Cauchy criterion and therefore converges.

cards.title: Theorem 3.47: Addition and Scalar Multiplication of Series
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.47 (Addition and Scalar Multiplication of Series):
If $\sum a_n = A$ and $\sum b_n = B$, prove that $\sum (a_n + b_n) = A + B$, and $\sum c a_n = c A$ for any fixed constant $c$.
cards.back_html:
Let $A_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k$ and $B_n = \sum_{k=0}^n b_k$.

Then $A_n + B_n = \sum_{k=0}^n (a_k + b_k)$.

Since $\lim_{n\to\infty} A_n = A$ and $\lim_{n\to\infty} B_n = B$, by the algebraic properties of sequence limits:
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} (A_n + B_n) = A + B$$
The proof for $c A_n \to c A$ is even simpler.

cards.title: Theorem 3.50 (Mertens): Series Convolution & Setup
cards.front_html:
Definition & Theorem 3.50 (Mertens' Theorem on Series Convolution):
Given $\sum a_n = A$ and $\sum b_n = B$, define their product (convolution / Cauchy product) as $c_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}$.
If $\sum a_n$ converges absolutely, prove that $\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n = AB$.

Paso 1: Definir las sumas parciales y descomponer $C_n$:
cards.back_html:
Let $A_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k$, $B_n = \sum_{k=0}^n b_k$, $C_n = \sum_{k=0}^n c_k$, and $\beta_n = B_n - B \to 0$.

Expanding $C_n$:
$$\begin{aligned} C_n &= a_0 b_0 + (a_0 b_1 + a_1 b_0) + \dots + (a_0 b_n + a_1 b_{n-1} + \dots + a_n b_0) \\ &= a_0 B_n + a_1 B_{n-1} + \dots + a_n B_0 \\ &= a_0 (B + \beta_n) + a_1 (B + \beta_{n-1}) + \dots + a_n (B + \beta_0) \\ &= A_n B + a_0 \beta_n + a_1 \beta_{n-1} + \dots + a_n \beta_0 \end{aligned}$$
Put $\gamma_n = a_0 \beta_n + a_1 \beta_{n-1} + \dots + a_n \beta_0$. Since $A_n B \to AB$, it suffices to show $\lim_{n\to\infty} \gamma_n = 0$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.50 (Mertens): Proof of Limit gamma_n -> 0
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.50 (Mertens' Theorem):
Paso 2: Demostrar que $\gamma_n \to 0$ utilizando la convergencia absoluta de $\sum a_n$:
cards.back_html:
Put $\alpha = \sum_{n=0}^\infty |a_n| \lt \infty$ (by absolute convergence of $\sum a_n$).

Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, since $\beta_n \to 0$, choose $N$ such that $|\beta_n| \le \varepsilon$ for $n \ge N$. For $n \ge N$:
$$|\gamma_n| \le |\beta_0 a_n + \dots + \beta_N a_{n-N}| + |\beta_{N+1} a_{n-N-1} + \dots + \beta_n a_0| \le |\beta_0 a_n + \dots + \beta_N a_{n-N}| + \varepsilon \alpha$$
Keeping $N$ fixed and letting $n \to \infty$, since $a_k \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$:
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty} |\gamma_n| \le \varepsilon \alpha$$
Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, $\lim_{n\to\infty} \gamma_n = 0 \implies C_n \to AB$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.51 (Abel) & Remark on Series Convolution
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.51 (Abel's Theorem) & Remark on Series Convolution:
Enunciar el Teorema de Abel (3.51) e incluir las observaciones clave sobre la convolución de series y la necesidad de herramientas especializadas.
cards.back_html:
Theorem 3.51 (Abel's Theorem):
If the series $\sum a_n$, $\sum b_n$, and their convolution $\sum c_n$ (where $c_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}$) converge to $A$, $B$, and $C$ respectively, then $C = AB$.

Observaciones sobre la Convolución (Producto de Cauchy) de Series:

  • La convolución $c_n = \sum_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}$ representa el producto formal de dos series.
  • Si al menos una serie converge absolutamente, el Teorema de Mertens (3.50) garantiza que la convolución siempre converge al producto de los límites $AB$.
  • Sin convergencia absoluta, la serie convolución puede no converger. Sin embargo, si la convolución resulta convergente a un valor $C$, el Teorema de Abel (3.51) asegura que $C = AB$. La demostración de este resultado sin convergencia absoluta requiere herramientas especializadas del análisis real/complejo (específicamente la continuidad de las series de potencias en la frontera del disco de convergencia, Teorema 8.2 de Rudin).

cards.title: Theorem 3.54 (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem) — Statement & Decomposition
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.54 (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem) — Statement & Decomposition:
Let $\sum a_n$ be a conditionally convergent series of real numbers (converges, but not absolutely). Let $-\infty \le \alpha \le \beta \le \infty$.
State the theorem and define the non-negative and negative parts $p_n$ and $q_n$:
cards.back_html:
Enunciado: There exists a rearrangement $\sum a'_n$ with partial sums $s'_n$ such that:
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} s'_n = \alpha, \quad \limsup_{n\to\infty} s'_n = \beta$$
Paso 1 (Descomposición): Define $p_n = \frac{|a_n| + a_n}{2}$ and $q_n = \frac{|a_n| - a_n}{2}$.

Then $p_n - q_n = a_n$, $p_n + q_n = |a_n|$, with $p_n \ge 0$ and $q_n \ge 0$ for all $n$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.54 (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem) — Divergence of Parts
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.54 — Divergence of $\sum p_n$ and $\sum q_n$:
Paso 2: Demostrar que ambas series de términos no negativos $\sum p_n$ y $\sum q_n$ deben divergir a $+\infty$:
cards.back_html:
If both $\sum p_n$ and $\sum q_n$ converged, then $\sum (p_n + q_n) = \sum |a_n|$ would converge, contradicting that $\sum a_n$ is not absolutely convergent.

If $\sum p_n$ diverged and $\sum q_n$ converged (or vice versa), then $\sum a_n = \sum (p_n - q_n)$ would diverge, contradicting that $\sum a_n$ converges.

Therefore, both $\sum p_n$ and $\sum q_n$ must diverge to $+\infty$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.54 (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem) — Construction
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.54 — Construction of the Rearranged Series:
Paso 3: Definir las secuencias de términos no nulos $P_k, Q_k$ y describir la construcción inductiva del reordenamiento:
cards.back_html:
Let $P_1, P_2, P_3, \dots$ be the positive terms of $\sum a_n$ in order, and $Q_1, Q_2, Q_3, \dots$ be the absolute values of the negative terms of $\sum a_n$ in order. Since $\sum p_n, \sum q_n$ diverge, $\sum P_k = \infty$ and $\sum Q_k = \infty$.

Choose real sequences $\alpha_n \to \alpha$, $\beta_n \to \beta$ with $\alpha_n \lt \beta_n, \beta_1 \gt 0$.

Choose smallest $m_1, k_1$ such that:
$$P_1 + \dots + P_{m_1} \gt \beta_1, \quad P_1 + \dots + P_{m_1} - Q_1 - \dots - Q_{k_1} \lt \alpha_1$$
Then choose smallest $m_2, k_2$ to exceed $\beta_2$ and drop below $\alpha_2$, continuing indefinitely. This is possible since $\sum P_k = \infty$ and $\sum Q_k = \infty$.

cards.title: Theorem 3.54 (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem) — Convergence Bounds
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.54 — Proof of $\liminf s'_n = \alpha$ and $\limsup s'_n = \beta$:
Paso 4: Acotar las sumas parciales $x_n, y_n$ en los picos y valles y concluir el teorema:
cards.back_html:
Let $x_n, y_n$ be the partial sums of the constructed series ending at $P_{m_n}$ and $-Q_{k_n}$ respectively. By construction:
$$|x_n - \beta_n| \le P_{m_n}, \quad |y_n - \alpha_n| \le Q_{k_n}$$
Since $\sum a_n$ converges, $a_n \to 0$ (Theorem 3.23), so $P_k \to 0$ and $Q_k \to 0$ as $k \to \infty$.

Therefore, $x_n \to \beta$ and $y_n \to \alpha$.

Finally, no number smaller than $\alpha$ or larger than $\beta$ can be a subsequential limit of $s'_n$, establishing:
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty} s'_n = \alpha, \quad \limsup_{n\to\infty} s'_n = \beta$$

cards.title: Theorem 3.55: Invariance of Absolutely Convergent Series under Rearrangements
cards.front_html:
Theorem 3.55 (Rearrangement of Absolutely Convergent Series):
If $\sum a_n$ is a series of complex numbers which converges absolutely, prove that every rearrangement of $\sum a_n$ converges, and they all converge to the same sum.
cards.back_html:
Let $\sum a'_n$ be a rearrangement with partial sums $s'_n$, and let $s_n$ be the partial sums of $\sum a_n$.

Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, by absolute convergence (Theorem 3.22/3.45), choose $N$ such that for $m \ge n \ge N$:
$$\sum_{i=n}^m |a_i| \le \varepsilon$$
Choose $p$ such that the indices $1, 2, \dots, N$ are all contained in the first $p$ terms of the rearrangement $\{a'_1, \dots, a'_p\}$.

Then for any $n \gt p$, the terms $a_1, \dots, a_N$ cancel out in the difference $s_n - s'_n$, leaving only terms $a_k$ with $k \gt N$. Therefore:
$$|s_n - s'_n| \le \sum_{i=N+1}^\infty |a_i| \le \varepsilon$$
Hence $\{s'_n\}$ converges to the same sum as $\{s_n\}$.

cards.title: Elección de la división.
cards.front_html: Sea $f \in \mathscr B([a,b])$, y sea la división $P=\set{a=x_0\lt  \cdots \lt  x_n=b}$. ¿Que es una elección $C$ de la división?
cards.back_html:
Una elección $C=(c_i)_{i=1}^n$ es tal que $\forall_{i=1}^n c_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$.

O alternativamente para una partición, $\forall I \in P. c_I \in I$

cards.title: Suma de Riemann con elección.
cards.front_html: Sea $f \in \mathscr B([a,b])$, y sea la división $P=\set{a=x_0\lt  \cdots \lt  x_n=b}$ y sea $C$ una elección de $P$. ¿Cual es la Suma de Riemann?
cards.back_html: $$S(P, f, C, \alpha)=\sum_{I \in P}f(c_i)\alpha(I) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(c_i) \Delta\alpha_i$$

cards.title: Malla de una división.
cards.front_html: Sea la división $P=\set{a=x_0\lt  \cdots \lt  x_n=b}$. ¿Que es su malla?
cards.back_html:
$$\|P\|_\# = \sup (x_i-x_{i-1})$$
(Podria definirse con $\alpha$ pero esa definición no seria verdaderamente natural o algo)

cards.title: Integrabilidad
cards.front_html: Sea $f \in \mathscr B([a,b])$. ¿Como se define su integral?
cards.back_html: $$\int_A f\ \mathrm d\alpha= \biota I \in \mathbb R.\ \forall \varepsilon\gt 0\ \exists \delta\gt 0\ \forall P\ \forall C.\ \|P\|_\# \lt  \delta \implies |S(P, f, C, \alpha) - I|\lt \varepsilon$$

cards.title: Funciones Lipschitz
cards.front_html: Sea $f:X\to Y$ espacios metricos. ¿Que significa ser Lipschitz? ¿Cual es su constante de Lipschitz?
cards.back_html:
$$ \exists C\gt 0 \ \forall a,b \in X.\ d(f(a),f(b)) \le C \cdot d(a,b) $$ En ese caso, existe una menor constante $C$ la cual llamamos constante de Lipschitz. $$ C_f = \Set{\frac{d(f(a),f(b))}{d(a,b)} : a,b \in X, a\ne b} $$
Propiedad: Las funciones Lipschitz son automaticamente Uniformemente continuas con $\delta = \eps/C_f$

cards.title: Convolución de 2 series.
cards.front_html:
Sean $(a_i)_{i=0}^\infty$ y $(b_i)_{i=0}^\infty$ dos secuencias y las series formales respectivas $(\sum_{i=0}^n a_i)_n$ y $(\sum_{i=0}^n b_i)_n$.
¿Cual es su convolución? ¿Que es la serie producto?
cards.back_html:
La convolución $(a_i)_{i=0}^\infty * (b_i)_{i=0}^\infty = (c_i)_{i=0}^\infty$ esta dada por$$
c_n = \sum_{i=0}^n a_ib_{n-i}
$$
Mientras que la serie producto (Producto de Cauchy) es$$
\sum_{i=0}^\infty c_n
$$

cards.title: Cotas de Sumas de Riemann
cards.front_html:
Demostrar que para $f\in \mathscr B(I)$ tenemos que $$
L(P,f, \alpha) \le S(P,f, C, \alpha) \le U(P,f, \alpha)
$$
Y que ademas si $P'$ es refinamiento/mas fina que $P$ entonces
$$
L(P,f, \alpha) \le L(P', f, \alpha)
$$
$$
U(P',f, \alpha) \le U(P, f, \alpha)
$$
En resumen si $P'$ es el refinamiento comun de $P_1, P_2$:
$$
L(P_1,f, \alpha) \le S(P',f, C, \alpha) \le U(P_2,f, \alpha)
$$
cards.back_html:
Tenemos que $m_i \le f(x_i) \le M_i$, por lo tanto $\Delta \alpha_i$ es positivo mantiene orden, y sumatoria mantiene orden es decir$$
\sum_{i=1}^n m_i \Delta \alpha_i \le \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i) \Delta \alpha_i \le \sum_{i=1}^n M_i \Delta \alpha_i
$$
Lo cual demuestra la primera desigualdad. Luego si $P'$ es mas fina, entonces $I \subseteq J$ el unico intervalo que lo contiene, $$
m_J \le m_I \le M_I \le M_J
$$
Por lo tanto por inducción, si tenemos alguna partición (paso inductivo) donde $I_1 \cup I_2 = J$, entonces $\sum_{I \in P'} m_I \alpha(I) - \sum_{J \in P} m_J \alpha(J) = m_{I_1} \alpha(I_1) + m_{I_2} \alpha(I_2) - m_J \alpha(J) \ge 0$ y repetir al infinito. Entonces$$
L(P,f, \alpha) \le L(P', f, \alpha)
$$
De lo cual el resto se concluye.
(En la practica esta demostración es mas similar a un boceto)

cards.title: Integral Inferior y Superior.
cards.front_html: Sea $f\in \mathscr B(I)$. Demostrar $\underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha \le \overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha$
cards.back_html:
Por lo anterior sabemos$$
L(P_1,f,\alpha) \le U(P_2,f,\alpha)
$$
Aplicando $\sup, \inf$ respectivamente sobre las particiones:$$
\underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha \le \overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha
$$

cards.title: Condición de Darboux.
cards.front_html:
Demostrar$$
\underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha = \overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha \iff \forall \eps \gt  0\ \exists P.\ U(P,f, \alpha) - L(P, f, \alpha) \lt  \eps
$$
cards.back_html:
($\impliedby$) Tendremos que $\overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha - \underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha \le U(P,f, \alpha) - L(P, f, \alpha) \lt \eps$ para cualquier $\eps\gt 0$, asi que $\overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha = \underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha$.
($\implies$) $U(P_2,f, \alpha) - \overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha \lt \eps/2$ y $\underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d\alpha - L(P_1, f, \alpha)\lt \eps/2$, asi que si $P'$ es el refinamiento mutuo,$$ U(P',f, \alpha) - L(P',f,\alpha) \lt \eps $$

cards.title: Lemas de integrabilidad.
cards.front_html:
• Si $P' \supseteq P$ entonces$$ U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt \eps \implies U(P',f) - L(P',f) $$
  • Si $C_1, C_2$ son elecciones de la partición: $$ U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt \eps \implies |S(P,f,C_1) - S(P,f,C_2)| \lt \eps $$
  • Si $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ entonces:$$ U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt \eps \implies |S(P,f,C_1) - I| \lt \eps $$
cards.back_html:
Por refinamiento $L(P,f) \le L(P',f) \le U(P', f) \le U(P,f)$ y sale trivial.
$|S(P,f,C_1) - S(P,f,C_2)| \le U(P,f) - L(P,f)$ obvio.
$L(P,f) \le S, I \le U(P,f)$ implica la ultima.

cards.title: Darboux -> Riemann
cards.front_html: Si $I = \underline{\int_a^b} f = \overline{\int_a^b} f$ entonces $f \in \mathscr B(X)$ es Riemann integrable (clasica)
cards.back_html:
Asumimos que $f$ es Darboux integrable, entonces se tiene que $\forall \eps \gt  0 \ \exists P=(x_i)_{i=0}^n$ una partición tal que\[
U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt  \eps/2 
\]
Sea $P'=(y_k)_{k=0}^{n'}$ una partición con $$\|P'\| \lt  \min\left(\inf \Delta x_i, \frac{\eps/2}{(M-m)(n-1)} \right)$$

Entonces para $1 \le k \le n'$ con $n'$ la cantidad de puntos en la partición $P'$ pueden suceder solo dos situaciónes:
$$J = \set{k: \exists i \in \set{1,\cdots, n}.\ [y_{k-1}, y_k] \subseteq [x_{i-1}, x_i]}$$
$$G= P' \setminus J = \set{k: \exists i \in \set{1,\cdots, n}.\ x_i \in (y_{k-1}, y_k)}$$
Donde $|G| \le n-1$,
y designamos $P^*=(z_j)_{j=0}^{n^*}$ el refinamiento mutuo.
Ahora:\begin{align}
|I-S(P',f)| & \le |I-S(P^*,f)| + |S(P^*,f)-S(P',f)| \\
& \le |I-S(P,f)| + (M- m)\sum_{k \in G}\Delta y_k \\
& \lt  \eps
\end{align}

La demostración puede generalizarse

cards.title: Riemann -> Darboux
cards.front_html: Si $f \in \mathscr B(X)$ es Riemann integrable (clasica) entonces $\underline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d \alpha = \overline{\int_a^b} f\ \mathrm d \alpha$
cards.back_html:
Suponemos que $\exists I\in \mathbb R \ \forall \eps\gt 0 \ \exists \delta\gt 0$ tal que si $\|P\|\lt  \delta$ entonces para cualquier elección:\[
|I - S(P,f)| \lt  \eps/4
\]
Elegimos etiquetas tales que $M_i \ge f(t_i) \gt  M_i - \delta$ y $m_i + \delta \gt  f(s_i) \ge m_i$ con $\delta \lt  \frac{\alpha(X)}{4}\eps$, luego:\begin{align}
S(P,f, C_1) - S(P,f, C_2) &= \sum_{I \in P}(f(t_i)-f(s_i))\alpha(I) \\
& \gt  \sum_{I \in P}(M_i - \delta -m_i - \delta)\alpha(I) \\
& = U(P,f) - L(P,f) -2\delta\alpha(X) \\
\end{align}
Luego$$
U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt  \eps/2 + \eps/2 \lt  \eps
$$

cards.title: Medida del singleton.
cards.front_html:
Sea $f \in \mathscr R_\alpha([a,b])$ (en el sentido de $P=\set{a=x_0 \lt \cdots \lt x_n=b}$)
Entonces para $s \in (a,b)$: $$ \begin{align} \alpha(s)-\alpha(s^-)\gt 0 &\implies f(s)=f(s^-) \\ \alpha(s^+)-\alpha(s)\gt 0 &\implies f(s^+)=f(s) \end{align} $$ Mientras que si $f \in \mathscr B([a,b])$ entonces para $s \in (a,b)$: $$ f \in \mathscr R_{\mathbb 1(a, \infty)}([a,b]) \impliedby f \text{ Continua en } s $$
cards.back_html:
($\implies$) suponiendo que no es continua $\exists \eps \gt 0\ \forall \delta \gt 0\ \exists x.\ s \lt x \lt s +\delta \land |f(x)-f(s)|\ge\eps$, y por otra parte $s \lt v \implies \alpha(v)-\alpha(s) \gt 0$, si alguna partición contiene a estos entonces$$ U-L \ge (M_v-m_v)(\alpha(v)-\alpha(s)) \gt 0 $$ Contradicción.

($\impliedby$) Si $P=\set{a\lt s \lt x \lt b}$ entonces$$ U - L =(M_2-m_2) \xrightarrow{x \to s}0 $$ Asi que tenemos integrabilidad, con $\int_{a}^b f(x) \mathrm d\mathbb 1_{(a, \infty)}(x)=f(s)$

cards.title: Integrable por divisiones -> integrable por particiones.
cards.front_html: Sea $f \in \mathscr B(X)$. Entonces si $f$ es integrable en terminos de divisiones, tambien lo es bajo particiones.
cards.back_html:
Si $\forall \eps\gt 0 \exists P=(x_i)_{i=0}^n$ tal que$$
U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt  \eps
$$
Definimos $$P^\square=G \cup H =\set{\set{x_i}}_{i=0}^n \cup \set{(x_{i-1},x_i)}_{i=1}^n$$
En ese caso: $\set{x_{i-1}}, (x_{i-1}, x_i) \subseteq [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ y por lo tanto $m_{H_i}, m_{G_i} \ge m_i$ y viceversa, Luego\begin{align}
U(P^\square, f) - L(P^\square, f) &=\sum_{I \in P^\square}(M_I-m_I)\alpha(I) \\
&=\sum_{i =1}^n (M_{H_i}-m_{H_i})\alpha(x_{i-1},x_i) + \sum_{i=0}^n(f(x_i)-f(x_i))\alpha\set{x_i} \\
&\le \sum_{i =1}^n (M_i-m_i)\Delta\alpha_i \lt  \eps
\end{align}
Por lo tanto es integrable.
Sabemos que
\begin{align}
\alpha(s)-\alpha(s^-)\gt 0
&\implies f(s)=f(s^-) \\
\alpha(s^+)-\alpha(s)\gt 0
&\implies f(s^+)=f(s)
\end{align}

Crearemos una nueva División $P'$ que aproveche esto. En el primer caso, añadimos para $\delta\gt 0$, $y_i = x_i - \delta \lt  x_i$, y en el segundo, $x_i\lt  x_i+\delta = z_i$, para esos casos, $y_i, z_i \leadsto x_i$, y por continuidad lateral, $\inf_{[y_i, x_i]}f(x) \leadsto f(x_i)$ etc. Luego por ejemplo,
\begin{align}
m_{i}^-\Delta \alpha_i^- &\leadsto f(x_i)\alpha\set{x_i} \\
m_{i}^+\Delta \alpha_i^+ &\leadsto f(x_i)\alpha\set{x_i} \\
m_{i}^-\Delta \alpha_i^-+m_{i}^+\Delta \alpha_i^+ &\leadsto f(x_i)\alpha\set{x_i}
\end{align}
para el caso 1,2 y ambos al mismo tiempo. Por el otro lado, los lados clasicos, donde esta vez tendremos
\begin{align}
\inf_{[x_{i-1}, y_i]} f(s)(\alpha(y_i)-\alpha(x_{i-1})) &\leadsto m_{H_i}\alpha(x_{i-1,}, x_i) \\
\inf_{[z_{i-1}, x_i]} f(s)(\alpha(x_i)-\alpha(z_{i-1})) &\leadsto m_{H_i}\alpha(x_{i-1,}, x_i) \\
\inf_{[z_{i-1}, y_i]} f(s)(\alpha(y_i)-\alpha(z_{i-1})) &\leadsto m_{H_i}\alpha(x_{i-1,}, x_i)
\end{align}
Para cada caso, asi$$
\lim_{\delta \downarrow 0} L(P', f) = L(P^\square, f)
$$
Pero $L(P',f) \le I \le U(P',f)$ asi tenemos
$$
L(P^\square, f) \le I \le U(P^\square, f)$$
Por lo tanto las integrales son iguales.

cards.title: Integrable por particiones -> Integrable por divisiones (con un pequeño caveat.)
cards.front_html:
Supongamos $f\in\mathscr B([a,b])$es integrable por particiones
y además
\begin{align}
\alpha(s)-\alpha(s^-)\gt 0
&\implies f(s)=f(s^-) \\
\alpha(s^+)-\alpha(s)\gt 0
&\implies f(s^+)=f(s)
\end{align}
Entonces $f$ es integrable por división, y las integrales coinciden.
cards.back_html:
Sea $P^\square=G \cup H =\set{\set{x_i}}_{i=0}^n \cup \set{(x_{i-1},x_i)}_{i=1}^n$ tal que \[ U(P^\square,f)-L(P^\square,f)\lt \varepsilon. \] Donde definimos $P'_\delta$ como en el inciso anterior. Si definimos $$ I^-=\sup_P L(P,f), \qquad I^+=\inf_P U(P,f), $$ entonces, para todo $\delta$, $$ L(P'_\delta,f)\leq I^+\leq I^- \leq U(P'_\delta,f). $$ Tomando $\delta\downarrow0$, $$ L(P^\square,f)\leq I^+\leq I^-\leq U(P^\square,f). $$ Por lo tanto, $$ I^+-I^- \leq U(P^\square,f)-L(P^\square,f) \lt \varepsilon. $$ Como $\varepsilon\gt 0$ es arbitrario, $$ I^+=I^-. $$ Luego $f\in\mathscr R_\alpha([a,b])$ y las integrales coinciden.
Es lamentable que ambas nociones no coincidan. Sin embargo tenemos una contención estricta, y la integral por particiones es una buena generalización, pues esta coincide con la integral de Lebesgue-Stieltjes bajo la medida $\alpha$ inducida.

cards.title: Theorem 6.8: Continuous Functions are Riemann-Stieltjes Integrable
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.8: Prove that if $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$.
cards.back_html:
Let $\varepsilon \gt 0$. Choose $\eta \gt 0$ so that $[\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)]\eta \lt \varepsilon$.

Since $f$ is continuous on the compact set $[a,b]$, $f$ is uniformly continuous on $[a,b]$ (Theorem 4.19), so there exists $\delta \gt 0$ such that $|f(x) - f(t)| \lt \eta$ whenever $|x - t| \lt \delta$.

If $P$ is any partition with $\Delta x_i \lt \delta$ for all $i$, then $M_i - m_i \le \eta$ ($i=1,\dots,n$).

Therefore:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) = \sum_{i=1}^n (M_i - m_i)\Delta\alpha_i \le \eta \sum_{i=1}^n \Delta\alpha_i = \eta[\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)] \lt \varepsilon$$
By Theorem 6.6, $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.9: Monotonic Functions with Continuous Integrator
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.9: Prove that if $f$ is monotonic on $[a,b]$ and $\alpha$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, then $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.
cards.back_html:
Let $\varepsilon \gt 0$. For any integer $n$, choose a partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ such that:
$$\Delta\alpha_i = \frac{\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)}{n} \quad (i = 1, \dots, n)$$
(This is possible since $\alpha$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ by the Intermediate Value Theorem).

Assuming $f$ is monotonically increasing, $M_i = f(x_i)$ and $m_i = f(x_{i-1})$. Then:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) = \frac{\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n [f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})] = \frac{\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)}{n} [f(b) - f(a)] \lt \varepsilon$$
for $n$ sufficiently large. By Theorem 6.6, $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.10: Finitely Many Discontinuities — Part 1: Covering Set E
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.10 (Part 1/2): Suppose $f$ is bounded on $[a,b]$, $f$ has only finitely many points of discontinuity, and $\alpha$ is continuous at every point at which $f$ is discontinuous.

Paso 1: Definir la cota $M$ y cubrir el conjunto finito de discontinuidades $E$:
cards.back_html:
Let $\varepsilon \gt 0$. Put $M = \sup |f(x)|$.

Let $E$ be the finite set of points at which $f$ is discontinuous.

Since $E$ is finite and $\alpha$ is continuous at every point of $E$, we can cover $E$ by finitely many disjoint closed subintervals $[u_j, v_j] \subset [a,b]$ such that:
$$\sum [\alpha(v_j) - \alpha(u_j)] \lt \varepsilon$$
Furthermore, we place these intervals such that every point of $E \cap (a,b)$ lies in the interior of some $[u_j, v_j]$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.10: Finitely Many Discontinuities — Part 2: Partition & Bound
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.10 (Part 2/2): Paso 2: Utilizar la compacidad del complemento $K = [a,b] \setminus \bigcup (u_j, v_j)$ y acotar $U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha)$:
cards.back_html:
Remove the open segments $(u_j, v_j)$ from $[a,b]$. The remaining set $K$ is compact.

Hence $f$ is uniformly continuous on $K$, so there exists $\delta \gt 0$ such that $|f(s) - f(t)| \lt \varepsilon$ if $s, t \in K$ and $|s - t| \lt \delta$.

Form a partition $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ containing all $u_j$ and $v_j$, with no points inside $(u_j, v_j)$, and with $\Delta x_i \lt \delta$ outside the intervals $[u_j, v_j]$.

Note that $M_i - m_i \le 2M$ for intervals $[u_j, v_j]$, and $M_i - m_i \le \varepsilon$ otherwise.

Therefore:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \le [\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)]\varepsilon + 2M\varepsilon$$
Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, Theorem 6.6 shows $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.11: Composition with Continuous Function — Part 1: Delta & Partition P
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.11 (Part 1/3): Suppose $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$, $m \le f \le M$, $\phi$ is continuous on $[m,M]$, and $h(x) = \phi(f(x))$.

Paso 1: Usar la continuidad uniforme de $\phi$ para elegir $\delta$ y seleccionar la partición $P$ para $f$:
cards.back_html:
Choose $\varepsilon \gt 0$. Since $\phi$ is continuous on the compact set $[m,M]$, $\phi$ is uniformly continuous on $[m,M]$.

Hence there exists $\delta \gt 0$ such that $\delta \lt \varepsilon$ and:
$$|\phi(s) - \phi(t)| \lt \varepsilon \quad \text{if } |s - t| \lt \delta \text{ and } s,t \in [m,M]$$
Since $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$, by Theorem 6.6 there exists a partition $P = \{x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\}$ of $[a,b]$ such that:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \lt \delta^2$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.11: Composition with Continuous Function — Part 2: Index Classes A & B
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.11 (Part 2/3): Paso 2: Dividir los subintervalos en las clases $A$ y $B$ y acotar las diferencias $M_i^* - m_i^*$:
cards.back_html:
Let $M_i, m_i$ be the bounds for $f$, and $M_i^*, m_i^*$ be the bounds for $h = \phi \circ f$.

Divide the indices $1, \dots, n$ into two classes:
  • $i \in A$ if $M_i - m_i \lt \delta$.
  • $i \in B$ if $M_i - m_i \ge \delta$.

For $i \in A$: $M_i^* - m_i^* \le \varepsilon$ (by choice of $\delta$).
For $i \in B$: $M_i^* - m_i^* \le 2K$, where $K = \sup |\phi(t)|$ for $m \le t \le M$.

Furthermore, $\delta \sum_{i \in B} \Delta\alpha_i \le \sum_{i \in B} (M_i - m_i)\Delta\alpha_i \lt \delta^2 \implies \sum_{i \in B} \Delta\alpha_i \lt \delta$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.11: Composition with Continuous Function — Part 3: Sum Bound & Conclusion
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.11 (Part 3/3): Paso 3: Acotar $U(P,h,\alpha) - L(P,h,\alpha)$ y concluir que $h = \phi \circ f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$:
cards.back_html:
Splitting the upper and lower sum difference into classes $A$ and $B$:
$$\begin{aligned} U(P,h,\alpha) - L(P,h,\alpha) &= \sum_{i \in A} (M_i^* - m_i^*) \Delta\alpha_i + \sum_{i \in B} (M_i^* - m_i^*) \Delta\alpha_i \\ &\le \varepsilon \sum_{i \in A} \Delta\alpha_i + 2K \sum_{i \in B} \Delta\alpha_i \\ &\le \varepsilon [\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)] + 2K\delta \\ &\lt \varepsilon [\alpha(b) - \alpha(a) + 2K] \end{aligned}$$
Since $\varepsilon$ was arbitrary, Theorem 6.6 implies that $h = \phi(f(x)) \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,b]$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.12: Properties of the Integral — Linearity & Order
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.12 (Properties of the Integral) — Statement & Proof of (a):
Enunciar las 5 propiedades (a-e) y demostrar la parte (a) (linealidad en el integrando):
  • (a) $f_1, f_2 \in \mathscr R(\alpha) \implies f_1 + f_2 \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ y $\int (f_1+f_2)d\alpha = \int f_1 d\alpha + \int f_2 d\alpha$; $cf \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ y $\int cf d\alpha = c \int f d\alpha$.
  • (b) $f_1 \le f_2 \implies \int f_1 d\alpha \le \int f_2 d\alpha$.
  • (c) Aditividad en dominios $[a,c]$ y $[c,b]$.
  • (d) $|f| \le M \implies |\int_a^b f d\alpha| \le M[\alpha(b)-\alpha(a)]$.
  • (e) Linealidad en el integrador $\alpha$.
cards.back_html:
Demostración de (a):
For $f = f_1 + f_2$ and any partition $P$:
$$L(P,f_1,\alpha) + L(P,f_2,\alpha) \le L(P,f,\alpha) \le U(P,f,\alpha) \le U(P,f_1,\alpha) + U(P,f_2,\alpha)$$
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, choose $P_1, P_2$ such that $U(P_j,f_j,\alpha) - L(P_j,f_j,\alpha) \lt \varepsilon$ ($j=1,2$). Replacing $P_1, P_2$ by their common refinement $P = P_1 \cup P_2$:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \lt 2\varepsilon \implies f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$$
Furthermore, $U(P,f_j,\alpha) \lt \int f_j d\alpha + \varepsilon$, so:
$$\int f d\alpha \le U(P,f,\alpha) \lt \int f_1 d\alpha + \int f_2 d\alpha + 2\varepsilon \implies \int f d\alpha \le \int f_1 d\alpha + \int f_2 d\alpha$$
Replacing $f_1, f_2$ by $-f_1, -f_2$ reverses the inequality $\implies \int (f_1+f_2) d\alpha = \int f_1 d\alpha + \int f_2 d\alpha$.

Observación: ¡Las demostraciones de las partes (b), (d) y (e) quedan como ejercicio para el lector! lol

cards.title: Theorem 6.12(c): Additivity over Subintervals [a,c] and [c,b]
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.12(c): Demostrar que si $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ en $[a,b]$ y $a \lt c \lt b$, entonces $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ en $[a,c]$ y en $[c,b]$, y:
$$\int_a^c f d\alpha + \int_c^b f d\alpha = \int_a^b f d\alpha$$
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, choose a partition $P^*$ of $[a,b]$ such that $U(P^*,f,\alpha) - L(P^*,f,\alpha) \lt \varepsilon$.

Form the refinement $P = P^* \cup \{c\}$ by adding the point $c$. By refinement properties:
$$U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \le U(P^*,f,\alpha) - L(P^*,f,\alpha) \lt \varepsilon$$
The partition $P$ splits into $P_1 = P \cap [a,c]$ (partition of $[a,c]$) and $P_2 = P \cap [c,b]$ (partition of $[c,b]$).

Since $U(P,f,\alpha) = U(P_1,f,\alpha) + U(P_2,f,\alpha)$ and $L(P,f,\alpha) = L(P_1,f,\alpha) + L(P_2,f,\alpha)$:
$$[U(P_1,f,\alpha) - L(P_1,f,\alpha)] + [U(P_2,f,\alpha) - L(P_2,f,\alpha)] = U(P,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \lt \varepsilon$$
Since both terms are non-negative, each is $\lt \varepsilon$, proving $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ on $[a,c]$ and $[c,b]$.

Furthermore:
$$\left| \int_a^c f d\alpha + \int_c^b f d\alpha - \int_a^b f d\alpha \right| \le U(P_1,f,\alpha) + U(P_2,f,\alpha) - L(P,f,\alpha) \lt \varepsilon$$
Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, equality $\int_a^c f d\alpha + \int_c^b f d\alpha = \int_a^b f d\alpha$ follows.

cards.title: Theorem 6.13: Products & Absolute Values of Integrable Functions
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.13: Si $f, g \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ en $[a,b]$, demostrar que:
(a) $fg \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$
(b) $|f| \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ y $\left|\int_a^b f d\alpha\right| \le \int_a^b |f| d\alpha$
cards.back_html:
Demostración de (a):
Taking $\phi(t) = t^2$, Theorem 6.11 shows $f^2 \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$ whenever $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.
Use the algebraic identity:
$$4fg = (f+g)^2 - (f-g)^2$$
Since $f+g$ and $f-g$ are in $\mathscr R(\alpha)$, their squares $(f+g)^2$ and $(f-g)^2$ are in $\mathscr R(\alpha)$. By linearity, $4fg \in \mathscr R(\alpha) \implies fg \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.

Demostración de (b):
Taking $\phi(t) = |t|$, Theorem 6.11 shows $|f| \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$.
Choose $c = \pm 1$ so that $c \int_a^b f d\alpha \ge 0$. Since $c f(x) \le |f(x)|$ for all $x \in [a,b]$:
$$\left|\int_a^b f d\alpha\right| = c \int_a^b f d\alpha = \int_a^b c f d\alpha \le \int_a^b |f| d\alpha$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.16: Integration with Respect to Point-Mass Series Integrator
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.16: Suppose $c_n \ge 0$, $\sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n$ converges, $\{s_n\}$ is a sequence of distinct points in $(a,b)$, $\alpha(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n I(x - s_n)$, and $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$. Demostrar que:
$$\int_a^b f d\alpha = \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n f(s_n)$$
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, choose $N$ such that $\sum_{N+1}^\infty c_n \lt \varepsilon$.

Split $\alpha = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$, where $\alpha_1(x) = \sum_{n=1}^N c_n I(x - s_n)$ and $\alpha_2(x) = \sum_{N+1}^\infty c_n I(x - s_n)$.

By Theorems 6.12 and 6.15 (finite point masses):
$$\int_a^b f d\alpha_1 = \sum_{n=1}^N c_n f(s_n)$$
Since $\alpha_2(b) - \alpha_2(a) = \sum_{N+1}^\infty c_n \lt \varepsilon$, by Theorem 6.12(d):
$$\left|\int_a^b f d\alpha_2\right| \le M\varepsilon \quad \text{where } M = \sup |f(x)|$$
Using $\alpha = \alpha_1 + \alpha_2$ and linearity (Theorem 6.12e):
$$\left| \int_a^b f d\alpha - \sum_{n=1}^N c_n f(s_n) \right| = \left| \int_a^b f d\alpha_2 \right| \le M\varepsilon$$
Letting $N \to \infty$, we obtain $\int_a^b f d\alpha = \sum_{n=1}^\infty c_n f(s_n)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.17: Reduction to Riemann Integral — Step 1: Partition & MVT
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.17 (Reduction to Riemann Integral):
Assume $\alpha$ increases monotonically, $\alpha' \in \mathscr R$ on $[a,b]$, and $f$ is bounded on $[a,b]$.
Prove that $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha) \iff f\alpha' \in \mathscr R$, and in that case $\int_a^b f d\alpha = \int_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x) dx$.

Paso 1: Aplicar el Criterio de Integrabilidad a $\alpha'$ y el Teorema del Valor Medio:
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, apply Theorem 6.6 to $\alpha'$: there is a partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ of $[a,b]$ such that:
$$U(P, \alpha') - L(P, \alpha') \lt \varepsilon$$
By the Mean Value Theorem applied to $\alpha$ on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$, there exist points $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ such that:
$$\Delta\alpha_i = \alpha'(t_i) \Delta x_i \quad (i = 1, \dots, n)$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.17: Reduction to Riemann Integral — Step 2: Bounding Sums
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.17: Paso 2: Acotar la diferencia entre la suma de Riemann-Stieltjes y la suma de Riemann para $f\alpha'$:
cards.back_html:
If $s_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$, then $\sum_{i=1}^n |\alpha'(s_i) - \alpha'(t_i)| \Delta x_i \lt \varepsilon$ (by $U(P,\alpha') - L(P,\alpha') \lt \varepsilon$).

Put $M = \sup |f(x)|$. Since $\sum_{i=1}^n f(s_i) \Delta\alpha_i = \sum_{i=1}^n f(s_i)\alpha'(t_i) \Delta x_i$, it follows that:
$$\left| \sum_{i=1}^n f(s_i) \Delta\alpha_i - \sum_{i=1}^n f(s_i)\alpha'(s_i) \Delta x_i \right| \le M\varepsilon$$
In particular, $\sum_{i=1}^n f(s_i) \Delta\alpha_i \le U(P, f\alpha') + M\varepsilon$ for all choices of $s_i$, so:
$$U(P, f, \alpha) \le U(P, f\alpha') + M\varepsilon$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.17: Reduction to Riemann Integral — Step 3: Reverse Inequality
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.17: Paso 3: Demostrar la desigualdad inversa y establecer $|U(P, f, \alpha) - U(P, f\alpha')| \le M\varepsilon$:
cards.back_html:
The same argument applied to the upper sum of $f\alpha'$ yields:
$$U(P, f\alpha') \le U(P, f, \alpha) + M\varepsilon$$
Combining both inequalities gives:
$$|U(P, f, \alpha) - U(P, f\alpha')| \le M\varepsilon$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.17: Reduction to Riemann Integral — Step 4: Upper/Lower Integrals Equality
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.17: Paso 4: Extender a refinamientos, igualar las integrales superiores e inferiores y concluir el teorema:
cards.back_html:
Note that $U(P,\alpha') - L(P,\alpha') \lt \varepsilon$ remains true if $P$ is replaced by any refinement, so $|U(P, f, \alpha) - U(P, f\alpha')| \le M\varepsilon$ holds for all refinements.

We conclude that:
$$\left| \overline{\int}_a^b f d\alpha - \overline{\int}_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x) dx \right| \le M\varepsilon$$
Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary:
$$\overline{\int}_a^b f d\alpha = \overline{\int}_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x) dx$$
The equality of lower integrals follows in exactly the same way. Thus $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha) \iff f\alpha' \in \mathscr R$, and $\int_a^b f d\alpha = \int_a^b f(x)\alpha'(x) dx$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.19: Change of Variable — Step 1: Partition Bijection & Sums
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.19 (Change of Variable in Riemann-Stieltjes Integrals):
Suppose $\varphi$ is a strictly increasing continuous function mapping $[A,B]$ onto $[a,b]$, $\alpha$ is monotonic increasing on $[a,b]$, $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$, $\beta(y) = \alpha(\varphi(y))$, $g(y) = f(\varphi(y))$.

Prove $g \in \mathscr R(\beta)$ and $\int_A^B g d\beta = \int_a^b f d\alpha$.
Paso 1: Correspondencia biyectiva entre particiones $P$ y $Q$ y las sumas superiores e inferiores:
cards.back_html:
To each partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ of $[a,b]$ corresponds a partition $Q = \{y_0, \dots, y_n\}$ of $[A,B]$ such that $x_i = \varphi(y_i)$.

Since $\varphi$ is a continuous strictly increasing bijection from $[A,B]$ onto $[a,b]$, all partitions of $[A,B]$ are obtained in this way.

The values taken by $f$ on $[x_{i-1}, x_i]$ are exactly the same as those taken by $g$ on $[y_{i-1}, y_i]$, and $\Delta\beta_i = \alpha(\varphi(y_i)) - \alpha(\varphi(y_{i-1})) = \alpha(x_i) - \alpha(x_{i-1}) = \Delta\alpha_i$.

Therefore:
$$U(Q, g, \beta) = U(P, f, \alpha), \quad L(Q, g, \beta) = L(P, f, \alpha)$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.19: Change of Variable — Step 2: Proof & Classic Formula
cards.front_html: Theorem 6.19: Paso 2: Concluir $\int_A^B g d\beta = \int_a^b f d\alpha$ y deducir la fórmula clásica del cambio de variable para integrales de Riemann:
cards.back_html:
Since $f \in \mathscr R(\alpha)$, $P$ can be chosen so that both $U(P, f, \alpha)$ and $L(P, f, \alpha)$ are arbitrarily close to $\int_a^b f d\alpha$.

Combined with $U(Q, g, \beta) = U(P, f, \alpha)$ and Theorem 6.6, this proves $g \in \mathscr R(\beta)$ and:
$$\int_A^B g d\beta = \int_a^b f d\alpha$$

Caso Especial (Cambio de variable de Riemann):
Take $\alpha(x) = x \implies \beta = \varphi$. If $\varphi' \in \mathscr R$ on $[A,B]$, applying Theorem 6.17 to the left side yields:
$$\int_a^b f(x) dx = \int_A^B f(\varphi(y)) \varphi'(y) dy$$

cards.title: Theorem 6.20: FTC Part I — Step 1: Uniform Continuity of F
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.20 (FTC Part I) — Step 1: Uniform Continuity:
Let $f \in \mathscr R$ on $[a,b]$. For $a \le x \le b$, put $F(x) = \int_a^x f(t) dt$.
Demostrar que $F$ es uniformemente continua en $[a,b]$:
cards.back_html:
Since $f \in \mathscr R$, $f$ is bounded. Suppose $|f(t)| \le M$ for $a \le t \le b$.

If $a \le x \lt y \le b$, then by Theorem 6.12(c) and (d):
$$|F(y) - F(x)| = \left| \int_x^y f(t) dt \right| \le M(y - x)$$
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, we see that $|F(y) - F(x)| \lt \varepsilon$ provided that $|y - x| \lt \varepsilon / M$.

This proves continuity (and in fact, uniform continuity) of $F$ on $[a,b]$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.20: FTC Part I — Step 2: Differentiability F'(x0) = f(x0)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.20 (FTC Part I) — Step 2: Differentiability:
Demostrar que si $f$ es continua en $x_0 \in [a,b]$, entonces $F$ es derivable en $x_0$ y $F'(x_0) = f(x_0)$:
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, since $f$ is continuous at $x_0$, choose $\delta \gt 0$ such that $|f(t) - f(x_0)| \lt \varepsilon$ if $|t - x_0| \lt \delta$ and $a \le t \le b$.

Hence, if $x_0 - \delta \lt s \le x_0 \le t \lt x_0 + \delta$ and $a \le s \lt t \le b$, we have by Theorem 6.12(d):
$$\left| \frac{F(t) - F(s)}{t - s} - f(x_0) \right| = \left| \frac{1}{t - s} \int_s^t [f(u) - f(x_0)] du \right| \lt \varepsilon$$
It follows that $F'(x_0) = f(x_0)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.21: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (Part II)
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.21 (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Part II):
If $f \in \mathscr R$ on $[a,b]$ and if there is a differentiable function $F$ on $[a,b]$ such that $F' = f$, prove that:
$$\int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)$$
cards.back_html:
Given $\varepsilon \gt 0$, choose a partition $P = \{x_0, \dots, x_n\}$ of $[a,b]$ so that $U(P,f) - L(P,f) \lt \varepsilon$.

The Mean Value Theorem furnishes points $t_i \in [x_{i-1}, x_i]$ such that:
$$F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = F'(t_i) \Delta x_i = f(t_i) \Delta x_i \quad (i = 1, \dots, n)$$
Summing over $i$:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n f(t_i) \Delta x_i = F(b) - F(a)$$
Since $\sum f(t_i) \Delta x_i$ and $\int_a^b f(x) dx$ both lie between $L(P,f)$ and $U(P,f)$, Theorem 6.7(c) yields:
$$\left| F(b) - F(a) - \int_a^b f(x) dx \right| \lt \varepsilon$$
Since this holds for every $\varepsilon \gt 0$, the proof is complete: $\int_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)$.

cards.title: Theorem 6.22: Integration by Parts
cards.front_html:
Theorem 6.22 (Integration by Parts):
Suppose $F$ and $G$ are differentiable functions on $[a,b]$, $F' = f \in \mathscr R$, and $G' = g \in \mathscr R$. Prove that:
$$\int_a^b F(x)g(x) dx = F(b)G(b) - F(a)G(a) - \int_a^b f(x)G(x) dx$$
cards.back_html:
Put $H(x) = F(x)G(x)$. By the product rule for derivatives, $H'(x) = F'(x)G(x) + F(x)G'(x) = f(x)G(x) + F(x)g(x)$.

By Theorem 6.13, products of integrable functions are integrable, so $H' \in \mathscr R$.

Apply Theorem 6.21 (FTC Part II) to $H$ and its derivative $H'$:
$$\int_a^b H'(x) dx = H(b) - H(a) \implies \int_a^b [f(x)G(x) + F(x)g(x)] dx = F(b)G(b) - F(a)G(a)$$
By linearity of the integral (Theorem 6.12a):
$$\int_a^b F(x)g(x) dx = F(b)G(b) - F(a)G(a) - \int_a^b f(x)G(x) dx$$

cards.title: Series de funciones.
cards.front_html: Sean $(f_n)_n$ una secuencia de funciones tales que $\forall n \in \mathbb N.\ f_n:X \to V$ desde un espacio metrico a uno normado. Cual es la serie y cuando hay convergencia?
cards.back_html: Definimos $S_n(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)$, entonces $S(x)=\lim_{n\to\infty}S_n(x)$ si este converge.

cards.title: Procedure: Add Common Hypothesis (.d)
cards.front_html:
Procedure: Add Common Hypothesis (.d)
Let $\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_n, \mathrm{B}$ be formulas. Given a proof for $\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_n \vdash \mathrm{B}$, find a proof for:
$$((\gm \lthen \mathrm{A}_1), \dots, (\gm \lthen \mathrm{A}_n) \vdash (\gm \lthen \mathrm{B}))$$
cards.back_html:
Proof by induction on proof step time:
Time 0: Axioms/rules use Added Hypothesis Forms (ax-1.a, ax-2.a, ax-3.a).
Time k: Replace every previously proven theorem $\mathrm{X}_1, \dots \vdash \mathrm{Y}$ step with its hypothesis form $\gm \lthen \mathrm{X}_1, \dots \vdash \gm \lthen \mathrm{Y}$ (denoted .d).

cards.title: Deductive Forms
cards.front_html:
Deductive Forms:
$$\begin{align*} \gm \lthen \ph & \vdash \gm \lthen (\ps \lthen \ph) && \text{(ax-1.d)} \\ \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) & \vdash \gm \lthen ((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch)) && \text{(ax-2.d)} \\ \ta \lthen (\gm \lthen \ph), \ \ta \lthen (\gm \lthen (\ph \lthen \ps)) & \vdash \ta \lthen (\gm \lthen \ps) && \text{(mpdd)} \\ \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen \ps), \ \gm \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) & \vdash \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch) && \text{(syld)} \\ \gm \lthen \ps, \ \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) & \vdash \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch) && \text{(mpid)} \end{align*}$$
Find the proof of at least one.
cards.back_html:
Proof of ax-1.d:
$$\begin{align*} 1. & \quad \gm \lthen \ph && \text{(assumed)} \\ 2. & \quad \gm \lthen (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ph)) && \text{(ax-1.a)} \\ 3. & \quad \gm \lthen (\ps \lthen \ph) && \text{(ax-mpd / mpd, 1, 2)} \end{align*}$$

cards.title: imim1i
cards.front_html:
Partially Closed Syllogism (imim1i):
$$(\ph \lthen \ps) \vdash (\ps \lthen \ch) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch)$$

cards.title: Procedure: Deduction Theorem (DT)
cards.front_html:
Procedure: Deduction Theorem (DT)
If $\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_{n-1}, \mathrm{A}_n \vdash \mathrm{B}$, then:
$$\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_{n-1} \vdash \mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{B}$$
cards.back_html:
By Add Common Hypothesis with $\gm = \mathrm{A}_n$, we obtain:
$(\mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{A}_1), \dots, (\mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{A}_{n-1}), (\mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{A}_n) \vdash (\mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{B})$
Using ax-1.i and id ($\vdash \mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{A}_n$), we simplify to:
$$\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_{n-1} \vdash \mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{B}$$

cards.title: Procedure: Theorem to Closed Form
cards.front_html:
Procedure: Theorem to Closed Form
Given proof $\mathrm{A}_1, \dots, \mathrm{A}_n \vdash \mathrm{B}$, reduce to proposition:
$$\vdash \mathrm{A}_1 \lthen (\dots \lthen (\mathrm{A}_n \lthen \mathrm{B}))$$
cards.back_html: Apply the Deduction Theorem (DT) repeatedly to eliminate antecedents one by one.

cards.title: Applying Deduction Theorem
cards.back_html:
Pons:
$$\begin{align*} 1. & \quad \ph, \ \ph \lthen \ps \vdash \ps && \text{(ax-mp)} \\ 2. & \quad \ph \vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ps && \text{(DT)} \\ 3. & \quad \vdash \ph \lthen ((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ps) && \text{(DT)} \end{align*}$$
imim1:
$$\begin{align*} 1. & \quad \ph \lthen \ps, \ \ps \lthen \ch \vdash \ph \lthen \ch && \text{(syll)} \\ 2. & \quad \ph \lthen \ps \vdash (\ps \lthen \ch) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch) && \text{(DT)} \\ 3. & \quad \vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen ((\ps \lthen \ch) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch)) && \text{(DT)} \end{align*}$$
Swap:
$$\begin{align*} 1. & \quad \ps, \ \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) \vdash \ph \lthen \ch && \text{(mpi)} \\ 2. & \quad \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) \vdash \ps \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch) && \text{(DT)} \\ 3. & \quad \vdash (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) \lthen (\ps \lthen (\ph \lthen \ch)) && \text{(DT)} \end{align*}$$

cards.title: ImpCon
cards.front_html:
Remark (The implicational Conjunction):
The following theorems feature a particularly interesting mix of negation and implication, namely $ eg(\ph \lthen eg \ps)$, joining together WFF $\ph$ and $\ps$. This is a natural target to define $\ph \land \ps$ later on.

Theorem (ImpCon): An implicational conjunction
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen eg(\ph \lthen eg \ps)))$$
cards.back_html:
$$ egin{align*}
1. & \quad \ph \lthen ((\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen 
eg \ps) && 	ext{(pons)} \
2. & \quad \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen 
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps)) && 	ext{(con2.d, 1)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: jcn
cards.front_html:
jcn (ImpCon with alternate negation):
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen (\neg \ps \lthen \neg(\ph \lthen \ps)))$$

cards.title: Undo Conjunction
cards.back_html:
Begin with either (scotus) $\vdash eg \ph \lthen (\ph \lthen \ps)$, or (ax-1) $\vdash eg \ps \lthen (\ph \lthen eg\ps)$.

Then apply (con2i) so (1) $\vdash eg(\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ph$, and (2) $\vdash eg(\ph \lthen eg \ps) \lthen \ps$, respectively.

Notice that for greater generality simplim has $\ps$ instead of $ eg \ps$, though if needed it can be instantiated as $ eg(\ph \lthen eg\ps) \lthen \ph$.

cards.title: impt
cards.front_html:
impt (Importation - Joins together two antecedents):
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) \lthen (\neg(\ph \lthen \neg \ps) \lthen \ch)$$
cards.back_html:
$$ egin{align*}
1. & \quad \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) && 	ext{(assumed)} \
2. & \quad \ph \lthen (
eg \ch \lthen 
eg \ps) && 	ext{(con3.d, 1)} \
3. & \quad 
eg \ch \lthen (\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) && 	ext{(Swap, 2)} \
4. & \quad 
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch && 	ext{(con2, 3)} \
5. & \quad \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) \vdash 
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch && 	ext{(tfore)} \
6. & \quad \vdash (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) \lthen (
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch) && 	ext{(DT)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: expt
cards.front_html:
expt (Exportation - Splits an antecedent into two):
$$\vdash (\neg(\ph \lthen \neg \ps) \lthen \ch) \lthen (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch))$$
cards.back_html:
$$ egin{align*}
1. & \quad 
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch && 	ext{(assumed)} \
2. & \quad 
eg \ch \lthen (\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) && 	ext{(con2, 1)} \
3. & \quad \ph \lthen (
eg \ch \lthen 
eg \ps) && 	ext{(Swap, 2)} \
4. & \quad \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) && 	ext{(con3.d, 3)} \
5. & \quad 
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch \vdash \ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch) && 	ext{(tfore)} \
6. & \quad \vdash (
eg(\ph \lthen 
eg \ps) \lthen \ch) \lthen (\ph \lthen (\ps \lthen \ch)) && 	ext{(DT)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: ja
cards.front_html:
ja (Converse of jarr and jarl):
$$(\neg \ph \lthen \ch), \ (\ps \lthen \ch) \vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ch$$
cards.back_html:
$$\begin{align*}
1. & \quad \neg \ph \lthen \ch && \text{(assumed)} \\
2. & \quad \ps \lthen \ch && \text{(assumed)} \\
3. & \quad \neg \ch \lthen \ph && \text{(con1i, 1)} \\
4. & \quad \neg \ch \lthen \neg \ps && \text{(con3i, 2)} \\
5. & \quad \neg \ch \lthen \neg(\ph \lthen \ps) && \text{(jcn.d, 3, 4)} \\
6. & \quad (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ch && \text{(con4i, 5)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: Cases
cards.front_html:
Cases (Prove by Cases):
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen (( \neg \ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \ps)$$
cards.back_html:
Because of ja, $(\neg \ph \lthen \ps), \ (\ph \lthen \ps) \vdash (\ph \lthen \ph) \lthen \ps$.
Then use id and the Deduction Theorem.

cards.title: Contradiction (pm265)
cards.front_html:
Contradiction / pm265 (Prove by Contradiction):
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen ((\ph \lthen \neg \ps) \lthen \neg \ph)$$
cards.back_html:
Likewise, $( eg \ps \lthen eg \ph), \ (\ps \lthen eg \ph) \vdash (\ps \lthen \ps) \lthen eg \ph$.
Then apply con4, con2, id, and the Deduction Theorem.

cards.title: df-bi (Basic Definition)
cards.front_html:
Definition of Biconditional (IFF):
Define $\ph \liff \ps$ using implication and negation.
cards.back_html: $$\neg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \neg(\ps \lthen \ph))$$

cards.title: df-an
cards.front_html: Definition of conjunction $\ph \land \ps$
cards.back_html: $$\neg(\ph \lthen \neg\ps)$$

cards.title: df-or
cards.front_html: Definition of disjunction $\ph \lor \ps$
cards.back_html: $$\neg\ph \lthen \ps$$

cards.title: Generalized Implication (df-nd)
cards.front_html:
Definition of generalized implication$$
\ph_1 , \cdots, \ph_n \implies \ps
$$
cards.back_html:
$$
(\ph_1 \land\cdots \land \ph_n) \lthen \ps
$$

cards.title: df-bi (The Big Formula Axiom)
cards.front_html:
The Big Formula Axiom (df-bi):
To define $\ph \liff \ps$ non-self-referentially without introducing external axioms.
cards.back_html:
Let $\Phi(\ph,\ps)$ abbreviate $\neg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \neg(\ps \lthen \ph))$.

Add the axiom:
$$\vdash \neg(((\ph \liff \ps) \lthen \Phi(\ph,\ps)) \lthen \neg(\Phi(\ph,\ps) \lthen (\ph \liff \ps)))$$
This single formula allows defining $\ph \liff \ps$ formally while avoiding self-reference and extra external language.

cards.title: impbi
cards.front_html:
Theorem (impbi): Introduce biconditional
$$\vdash (\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen ((\ps \lthen \ph) \lthen (\ph \liff \ps))$$

cards.title: dfbi1
cards.front_html:
Theorem (dfbi1): Recover underlying definition of biconditional
$$\vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \liff \neg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen \neg(\ps \lthen \ph))$$
cards.back_html:
$$ egin{align*}
1. & \quad 
eg(((\ph \liff \ps) \lthen \Phi(\ph,\ps)) \lthen 
eg(\Phi(\ph,\ps) \lthen (\ph \liff \ps))) && 	ext{(df-bi)} \
2. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen 
eg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen 
eg(\ps \lthen \ph)) && 	ext{(simplim, 1)} \
3. & \quad 
eg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen 
eg(\ps \lthen \ph)) \lthen (\ph \liff \ps) && 	ext{(simprim, 1)} \
4. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \liff 
eg((\ph \lthen \ps) \lthen 
eg(\ps \lthen \ph)) && 	ext{(impbi, 2, 3)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: biimp
cards.front_html:
Theorem (biimp): Get implication from biconditional
$$\vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ps)$$

cards.title: biimpr
cards.front_html:
Theorem (biimpr): Get opposite implication from biconditional
$$\vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (\ps \lthen \ph)$$

cards.title: Characterization of biconditional
cards.front_html: Axiomatic Definition & Characterization of Biconditional

cards.title: biid
cards.front_html:
Biconditional Reflexivity (biid):
$$\vdash \ph \liff \ph$$
cards.back_html: Use id ($\vdash \ph \lthen \ph$) and impbi.

cards.title: bitri
cards.front_html:
Biconditional Transitivity (bitri):
$$\ph \liff \ps, \ \ps \liff \ch \vdash \ph \liff \ch$$
cards.back_html:
By biimp and syll, $\ph \lthen \ps, \ps \lthen \ch \vdash \ph \lthen \ch$.
Similarly by biimpr and syll, $\ch \lthen \ph$.
By impbi, $\ph \liff \ch$.

cards.title: notbi
cards.front_html:
Biconditional Contraposition (notbi):
$$\vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \liff (\neg \ph \liff \neg \ps)$$
cards.back_html:
$$ egin{align*}
1. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (\ph \lthen \ps) && 	ext{(biimp)} \
2. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (\ps \lthen \ph) && 	ext{(biimpr)} \
3. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (
eg\ps \lthen 
eg\ph) && 	ext{(con3.d, 1)} \
4. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (
eg\ph \lthen 
eg\ps) && 	ext{(con3.d, 2)} \
5. & \quad (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (
eg\ph \liff 
eg\ps) && 	ext{(impbi.d, 3, 4)} \
6. & \quad (
eg\ph \liff 
eg\ps) \lthen (\ph \liff \ps) && 	ext{(using con4)} \
7. & \quad \vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \liff (
eg\ph \liff 
eg\ps) && 	ext{(impbi, 5, 6)}
\end{align*}$$

cards.title: Procedure: Propositional Replacement (PR)
cards.front_html:
Procedure: Propositional Replacement (PR)
If $\mathrm A(\ph)$ is a WFF where $\ph$ may appear, and $\mathrm A(\ps)$ is the formula with $\ps$ substituted for $\ph$, then:
$$\vdash (\ph \liff \ps) \lthen (\mathrm A(\ph) \liff \mathrm A(\ps))$$
cards.back_html:
Proof by structural induction:
Time 0: Base cases $\mathrm A(\ph) = \ph$ (uses id) or $\mathrm A(\ph) = \ch$ (uses ax-1).
Time k: Inductive step for compound formulas $\mathrm B(\ph) \lthen \mathrm C(\ph)$ (uses imim12.d and impbi.d) and $\neg \mathrm B(\ph)$ (uses notbi).

cards.title: Carga Eléctrica
cards.front_html:
¿Que es? (Cualitativamente)

  • ¿Que permite?
  • Como se puede interpretar?
  • Asumiendo un sistema aislado:...?
cards.back_html:
Es una propiedad intrínseca de la materia.
  • Permite la existencia de fuerzas de atracción y repulsión. (Cargas de igual signo se repelen; cargas de signo opuesto se atraen.)
  • Las fuerzas provienen de un campo electromagnético y existen cargas positivas y negativas. Es decir, podemos considerarlo como una función $\mathbb R^3 \to \mathbb R$
  • Se conserva en un sistema aislado.

cards.title: Carga Fundamental y Coulomb.
cards.front_html: ¿Cual es la unidad de carga mas chica? ¿Que unidad de carga estandar usamos?
cards.back_html:
• Carga elemental: $e$
  • Unidad del Sistema Internacional (SI): Coulomb ($\text{C}$)

cards.title: Partículas Elementales
cards.front_html: Carga de particulas elementales.
cards.back_html:
Las partículas atómicas tienen los siguientes estados de carga:
  • Protón: Carga positiva, $q = +e$
  • Electrón: Carga negativa, $q = -e$
  • Neutrón: Neutro, $q = 0$

cards.title: Carga Neta
cards.front_html: ¿Que es? ¿Es "Cuantica"?
cards.back_html:
Representa la carga total que posee un cuerpo en función del número de protones ($N_p$) y electrones ($N_e$).

Fórmula:
$Q = e(N_p - N_e)$
  • Si $N_p \neq N_e \implies$ Cuerpo cargado.
  • Si $N_p = N_e \implies$ Cuerpo neutro ($Q = 0$).
Notese que por cuantización, $N_p, N_e \in \mathbb N$ y por lo tanto $N \in \mathbb Z$.

cards.title: Densidades Continuas de Carga
cards.front_html: Modelos matemáticos para distribuciones continuas de carga según su geometría
cards.back_html:
• Lineal ($\lambda$): $\lambda = \frac{\mathrm d q}{\mathrm dl} \quad \left[\frac{\text{C}}{ \text{m}} \right]$
  • Superficial ($\sigma$): $\sigma = \frac{\mathrm d q}{\mathrm dA} \quad \left[\frac{\text{C}}{ \text{m}^2} \right]$
  • Volumétrica ($\rho$): $\rho = \frac{\mathrm d q}{\mathrm dV} \quad \left[\frac{\text{C}}{ \text{m}^3} \right]$

cards.title: Clasificación de los materiales
cards.front_html: ¿Como se clasifican los materiales segun conductividad?
cards.back_html:
• Conductores: Presentan libre movimiento de electrones.
  • Aislantes: No presentan movimiento de electrones.
  • Semiconductores: El movimiento de electrones es controlable/modulable.
  • Superconductores: A bajas temperaturas no presentan resistencia eléctrica.

cards.title: Teorema de Stokes-Cartan.
cards.front_html: Enunciar el Teorema de Stokes-Cartan.
cards.back_html:
Sea $ \Omega $⁠ un Manifold n-dimensional orientado con frontera. Donde $\partial \Omega$ tiene la orientación inducida .
Sea $\omega$ una $(n-1)$-forma suave con soporte compacto en $\Omega$. Entonces: $$ \int_{\Omega}\mathrm d\omega = \int_{\boldsymbol\partial \Omega} \omega $$
No siempre se requieren todas las condiciones, ie, la forma puede ser meramente diferenciable (TFC), pero la mayoria se requieren en general. (por ejemplo, que haya frontera y sea orientable).

cards.title: Ley de Coulomb
cards.front_html:
Enunciado Ley de Coulomb.

¿Cual sera la fuerza ejercida sobre la segunda carga por la primera?
cards.back_html:
Para cargas $q_1, q_2$ a una distancia $d$ la magnitud de la fuerza entre ellas es:$$
K_\eps\abs{\frac{q_1q_2}{d^2}} = \frac{1}{4\pi\eps_0}\abs{\frac{q_1q_2}{d^2}}
$$

La fuerza $\vec F_2$ ejercida sobre la segunda carga sera$$
\frac{1}{4\pi\eps_0}\frac{q_1q_2}{d^2} \cdot\frac{\vec r_2-\vec r_1}{|\vec r_2-\vec r_1|} = 
\frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\eps_0} \cdot\frac{\vec r_2-\vec r_1}{|\vec r_2-\vec r_1|^3} = \frac{q_1q_2}{4\pi\eps_0} \cdot\frac{\hat r_{12}}{|r_{12}|^2}
$$
Notese el signo. Si ambas son del mismo signo, es repulsiva, de otra forma, sera atractiva.

cards.title: Constante de Coulomb vs Permisividad del vacio.
cards.front_html: (Unidades y relación, no memorizar valor exacto).
cards.back_html:
$$
K_\eps \approx 8.988\times 10^9 \frac{\mathrm{Nm}^2}{\mathrm{C}^2}
$$
$$
\eps_0 \approx 8.854\times 10^{-12} \frac{\mathrm{C}^2}{\mathrm{Nm}^2}
$$

$$
K_\eps = \frac{1}{4\pi \eps_0}$$

cards.title: Fuerza ejercida sobre una carga de prueba
cards.front_html: Considere las cargas fijas $q_1, \cdots, q_n$ que ejercen sobre una carga de prueba $Q$. ¿Como se expresa esa fuerza?
cards.back_html:
$$
\vec F_Q = \frac{Q}{4\pi\eps_0}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i\frac{\hat r_i}{r_i^2} =\frac{Q}{4\pi\eps_0}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i\frac{\vec r_Q - \vec r_i}{\|\vec r_Q - \vec r_i\|^3}
$$
(recordar que $\hat r$ es el vector unitario y $r$ es su escalar.)

cards.title: Campo Electrico por una medida de cargas.
cards.front_html: Considere una ¿medida con signo? de carga $q$. Definición del campo vectorial electrico definido sobre $\Omega$ ejercido.
cards.back_html:
$$
\vec E(\vec r) = \frac{1}{4\pi\eps_0}\int_{\Omega} \frac{\vec r - \vec x}{|\vec r - \vec x|^3} \mathrm dq(\vec x)
$$
Donde $$
\mathrm dq(\vec x) = \begin{cases}
\lambda \mathrm dl &: \text{Curva} \\
\sigma \mathrm dS &: \text{Superficie} \\
\rho \mathrm dV &: \text{Volumen}
\end{cases}$$
O alternativamente en una carga discreta, se recupera la definición de suma.

cards.title: Teorema de Green.
cards.front_html: Demostrar el Teorema de Green.
cards.back_html:
Consideramos $F = (P, Q)$ con $\d \mathbf r = (\d x, \d y)$, entonces $\omega = F\cdot \d \mathbf r$
Ahora bien, la derivada exterior \begin{align}
\d \omega &= \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\d y\wedge \d x + \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\d x\wedge \d y \\
&= \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \d x\wedge \d y
\end{align}

$$
\implies \int_{\partial S} P\,\d x+ Q\, \d y = 
\int_S \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right) \d x\wedge \d y
$$
Donde $S$ es una superficie, y $\partial S$ es su frontera. $\d x \wedge \d y$ se traduce a integración clasica y no necesitamos hacer nada mas.

cards.title: Stokes paso 1: Aplicar Green.
cards.front_html: Sea $F = (P(x,y,z), Q(x,y,z), R(x,y,z)) $ y sea $S$ una superficie parametrizada por $f:D \subseteq \mathbb R^2 \to S \subseteq \mathbb R^3$ suave.
cards.back_html:
Si
\(
f(u,v)=
\bigl(x(u,v),y(u,v),z(u,v)\bigr).
\)
Entonces
\[
Df_{(u,v)} =
\begin{pmatrix}
x_u & x_v\\
y_u & y_v\\
z_u & z_v
\end{pmatrix}
\]
Luego
\(
\mathbf F\circ f
=

(P\circ f,Q\circ f,R\circ f)
\) y podemos considerar:
\(
\d\mathbf r
 =
Df
\begin{pmatrix}
du\\
dv
\end{pmatrix}
\)
, luego:

\[
\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r
=

(\mathbf F\circ f)
Df
\begin{pmatrix}
du\\
dv
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Sean
\(
(A,B)
=

(\mathbf F\circ f)Df.
\) La integral se vuelve:
\[
\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot \d\mathbf r
=

\oint_{\partial S}
A\,\d u+B\,\d v = \iint_S
\left(
\frac{\partial B}{\partial u}
-
\frac{\partial A}{\partial v}
\right)
\,\d u\wedge\d v
\]

Solo necesitamos entonces:

\[
\mathrm D_u B - \mathrm D_v A
\]

cards.title: Stokes paso 2: Regla de la cadena.
cards.front_html: Casos especiales de Stokes

cards.title: Stokes paso 3: Conclusión
cards.front_html: Casos especiales de Stokes
cards.back_html:
$\vec a^{\top}A\vec b = \sum_{i,j} a_i A_{ij}b_j$,
Luego\begin{align}
\vec a^{\top}A\vec b - \vec b^{\top}A\vec a &= \sum_{i,j} A_{ij}(a_ib_j - a_jb_i) \\
&= \sum_{1\le i\lt  j \le 3} (A_{ij}-A_{ji})(a_ib_j - a_jb_i) \\
&= \begin{pmatrix} A_{23} - A_{32} \\ A_{31} - A_{13} \\ A_{12} - A_{21}\end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} a_2b_3 - a_3b_2 \\ a_3b_1 - a_1b_3 \\ a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 \end{pmatrix} \\
&= 2\operatorname{Alt}(A)(\vec a, \vec b) = \operatorname{Axl} A \cdot \vec b \times \vec a
\end{align}
(Axl depende de la orientación elegida). Para nuestro caso, tenemos que, si $F=(P,Q,R)$ Entonces:$$
\operatorname{Axl}(\mathrm D F_{f(u,v)}) = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial R}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Q}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial P}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial R}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}-\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\end{pmatrix} = \nabla \times F_{f(u,v)}
$$
Asi que:
$$
D_2f_{(u,v)} \mathrm D F_{f(u,v)} D_1 f_{(u,v)} -  D_1f_{(u,v)} \mathrm D F_{f(u,v)}  D_2 f_{(u,v)} = \nabla \times F_{f(u,v)} \cdot D_1 f_{(u,v)} \times D_2f_{(u,v)}
$$
Entonces finalmente concluimos:\[
\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot \d\mathbf r
=
\iint_S
\nabla \times F_{f(u,v)} \cdot D_1 f_{(u,v)} \times D_2f_{(u,v)}
\,\d u\wedge\d v
\]
Pero $\d \mathbf S = D_1 f_{(u,v)} \times D_2f_{(u,v)}\,\d u\wedge\d v$, tenemos:\[
\oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot \d\mathbf r
=
\iint_S
\nabla \times F \cdot \d \mathbf S
\]
